title: Har Gow
subtitle: Cantonese steamed prawn dumplings with a translucent rice-flour skin
excerpt: Har gow are the benchmark dumpling of Cantonese dim sum, with a stretchy, slightly translucent skin made from wheat starch and tapioca starch wrapped around a juicy prawn filling. Getting the dough right takes practice, but the result is far better than anything from a packet. Makes 24 dumplings in about 90 minutes.
sourceNotes: Har gow originated in the teahouses of Guangzhou in the early twentieth century and is considered the dish by which a dim sum chef's skill is judged. The recipe is discussed in Yung Hei Yip's studies of Cantonese culinary tradition and appears in detailed form in Florence Lin's 'Florence Lin's Complete Book of Chinese Noodles, Dumplings and Breads' (William Morrow, 1986), which remains one of the most thorough English-language treatments of the technique.

recipe.freezeNotes: Arrange uncooked dumplings on a lined tray, freeze until solid, then transfer to a bag. Cook from frozen in a steamer for 12 to 14 minutes without defrosting.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The filling can be made up to 24 hours ahead and kept covered in the fridge. The dough must be made and used the same day.

glossaryTerms.definition: Also called tang mian flour, wheat starch is plain flour with the gluten removed. It produces a dough that turns translucent when steamed, which is the defining characteristic of har gow skins. It is sold in Chinese grocery shops and is not interchangeable with plain flour.

A Chinese technique in which raw protein, usually meat or prawns, is coated in a mixture of egg white, cornflour and sometimes bicarbonate of soda before cooking. The coating creates a silky, tender texture by protecting the protein from direct heat. In har gow it gives the prawn filling a bouncy snap.

The technique of folding a series of small, overlapping creases along the top edge of a dumpling to seal it and create a distinctive ridged shape. In har gow, the classic fold uses seven to ten pleats on one side only, which is the mark of a skilled dim sum chef.

content.text: This recipe makes 24 har gow and takes about 90 minutes from start to finish. The most difficult part is the
dough, which must be worked while hot and rested wrapped so it doesn't dry out. Once you have the texture right, the wrapping goes quickly.

step: the prawns are tossed with a little egg white and cornflour before the other ingredients go in. This is what gives har gow its characteristic snap when you bite through. Do not skip it. Each dumpling gets seven to ten pleats, created using the
technique, though even two or three pleats will seal the dumpling fine while you build confidence.

Make the filling first so it can chill while you work on the dough. Toss the {{raw-prawns}} with the {{egg-white}} and {{cornflour}} and leave for 10 minutes. Add the {{bamboo-shoots}}, {{sesame-oil}}, salt, sugar and white pepper. Mix well, cover and refrigerate.
Combine the {{wheat-starch}}, {{tapioca-starch}} and salt in a heatproof bowl. Pour the boiling water over in one go and stir immediately with a wooden spoon until a shaggy dough forms.

Add the {{lard}} and knead the dough in the bowl, or turn it onto a lightly oiled surface. Work for 3 to 4 minutes until smooth and pliable. The dough should feel like firm Play-Doh. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 10 minutes.

Divide the dough into 24 small balls, about 12g each. Keep them covered. Working one at a time, roll or press each ball into a circle about 8cm across. The skin should be thin enough to see your hand through it.

Place a teaspoon of filling just off-centre on the skin. Fold the skin over to form a half-moon and pinch the far edge firmly. Starting from one end, fold small pleats along the top curved edge, pressing each pleat against the flat back edge to seal. Aim for 7 pleats, or as many as you can manage.

Line the bamboo steamer with baking parchment or cabbage leaves. Bring water to a boil in a wok or wide pan. Arrange the dumplings with a little space between them, set the steamer over the water, cover and steam for 8 to 9 minutes until the skins are translucent and the filling is cooked through.
Serve immediately with soy sauce or chilli sauce for dipping. The skins toughen as they cool.

items.symptom: The dough is cracking when folded
items.cause: It dried out or was not worked enough while still warm
items.fix: Rub the surface with a tiny amount of oil and knead again. Keep unused dough covered with a damp cloth at all times. Work faster next time.

items.symptom: The skins are too thick and chewy after steaming
items.cause: The dough was rolled too thick, or there was too much tapioca starch
items.fix: Roll skins until almost translucent before filling. The skin should be no thicker than 2mm.

items.symptom: The dumplings are splitting open during steaming
items.cause: The seal was not pressed firmly, or the filling was too wet
items.fix: Press the pleated edge firmly. If the filling is weeping liquid, drain it before filling and reduce the filling amount slightly.

content.text: Har gow is central to yum cha, the Cantonese tradition of drinking tea and sharing small plates of dim sum. In Guangdong teahouses it is wheeled to the table on trolleys alongside siu mai and turnip cake. At home it is a project dish, usually made in large batches, and is a good test of dough technique. A dim sum chef is judged partly on how evenly they pleat har gow, but at home seven tidy pleats or even a crimped edge gets you exactly the same result in flavour.
